column2: Samuel identifies his divine sending to anoint Saul over Israel before commanding present attention to the Lord's voice; human you remains ordinary.
The Lord Sabaoth announces vengeance for Amalek's action and encounter on Israel's ascent from Egypt; the corporate singular pronouns remain.
Amalek and Jerim, everything possessed, prohibitions on preservation and sparing, destruction and the ban, and all four paired categories of victims remain in full.
column3: The selected Jerim is not silently removed as a presumed mistranscription; the violent command is translated without added detail or moral commentary in the text.

column2: The muster is at Gilgal with four hundred thousand troops and thirty thousand Judahite troops; neither figures nor place are harmonized to familiar alternatives.
column3: Troops for tagmata leaves the precise military grouping open rather than multiplying the numbers into invented unit sizes.

column2: Saul comes to plural Amalekite cities and ambushes in the wadi; the plural settlements and concealed military action remain.
The Kenite is commanded to depart lest Saul add him with Amalek; prior mercy to Israel on its ascent explains the exception, followed by withdrawal.
column3: Add you with him preserves the terse threat; destruction is contextually implied but not supplied as a new verb.

column2: The strike extends from Havilah to Shur facing Egypt; the selected territorial limits remain without adding a map identification.
Agag is captured alive while all Jerim's people are killed by the sword's edge; the contrast and Jerim recurrence remain.

Saul and all the people preserve Agag and good flocks, herds, foods, vineyards and all good things, contrasted with destroying despised things. Singular he was unwilling followed by plural they destroyed follows the selected shifts.
The Lord's word comes to Samuel and introduces the following direct speech; no content is moved out of verse 11.
The inherited consoled for parakeklemai remains distinct from the later regret verb; Saul's turning and failure to keep words explain the statement, and Samuel loses heart and cries all night.
column3: Consoled is a provisional lexical rendering with an evident contextual difficulty; possible relenting/regret senses need fuller lexical evidence. No reconciliation of divine emotion is asserted.

column2: Propose restoring behold at the encounter with the offering and naming Saul as its inferred actor for clarity. Meeting Israel, the report of Carmel, the erected hand, turned chariot, Gilgal and first spoils remain.
column3: The erected hand is retained without inserting monument into Scripture. Saul as offering subject is inferred from the approach to him and ensuing dialogue, not an explicit added Greek name.

column2: Saul blesses Samuel by the Lord and claims to have established everything spoken; the total claim remains available for the narrative's subsequent challenge.
Samuel challenges the claim through flock sound in his ears and oxen sound he hears; both audible animal groups remain.
Saul claims personal bringing and destruction while attributing preservation of the best animals to the people for the Lord your God; the shifts of agency and your remain.
Stop precedes Samuel's promise to report the night's divine speech, and the unnamed answering subject says Speak. The context identifies Saul without adding his name in the retained text.
Saul is small before Him and leader of a tribal division, then reminded of anointing over Israel. The selected before Him is not changed to in your own eyes.
column3: The compact relationship between small and leader remains provisional; no former-tense when you were small clause is imported.

column2: The mission is to destroy those sinning against Me, Amalek, and fight until finished; the selected direct divine first person and complete endpoint remain.
Failure to hear is contrasted with rushing for spoils and doing evil before the Lord; the accusation retains both acquisition and evaluation.
Because I listened to the people's voice follows the selected causal answer, then Saul claims the mission, Agag's capture and Amalek's destruction.
column3: People's voice is not changed to the Lord's voice or a denial of disobedience; the narrative's difficult self-justification is preserved.

column2: The people take flocks and cattle as first of the destruction-marked spoil to sacrifice before the Lord our God at Gilgal; our is retained distinctly from your in verse 15.

The question compares sacrifice with hearing, then behold introduces paired obedience/sacrifice and attentiveness/ram-fat contrasts. Authored line breaks make the existing parallel clauses audible without changing their words.
column3: Obedience is a contextual rendering of hearing; the poem does not authorize erasing sacrificial vocabulary elsewhere.

column2: Propose For to retain the explanatory opening before divination/sin and teraphim's sorrow and troubles. The causal rejection of the Lord's word and resulting rejection of Saul remain, with line breaks for the paired statements.
column3: Both nouns in the divination clause are anarthrous; inherited Divination is sin is retained provisionally rather than importing a comparison with rebellion from another text. Teraphim remains untranslated.

column2: Propose joining the confession to its explicit explanation with for: Saul sinned by transgressing both the Lord's word and Samuel's word because he feared and heard the people.
Saul asks Samuel to take away his sin and return for worship of the Lord your God; neither the petition's human addressee nor your is changed.
Samuel refuses return because Saul treated the divine word as nothing, with the same treatment predicted for Saul's kingship; the repeated contempt wording remains.
Samuel turns his face to leave; Saul seizes and tears the double cloak's edge. The named seizer and concrete garment image remain.
The Lord's tearing of the kingdom from Saul's hand today parallels the garment and precedes future giving to a better neighbor; no name is supplied for that neighbor.
Israel's future division in two precedes the denial of divine turning or changing mind, with the human comparison retained.
column3: The transition from Israel to inferred divine He is interpretive; the selected division clause is not replaced by a divine epithet or reconciled with verses 11 and 35.

column2: Saul repeats confession but seeks honor before Israel's elders and his people and Samuel's return for worship of the Lord your God; both audiences and possessives remain.
Samuel returns after Saul and an implicit subject bows to the Lord; the inherited he preserves the compressed subject sequence.
column3: Saul as worshiper fits the preceding request, while Samuel is the last explicit grammatical subject; this ambiguity remains open rather than silently renamed.

column2: Agag is summoned, approaches trembling and asks whether death is so bitter. Trembling and the question are retained rather than assurance that death has passed.
Samuel's childlessness comparison precedes slaughter of Agag before the Lord at Gilgal; the action is neither softened nor expanded into a more graphic method.
Samuel departs to Armathaim while Saul ascends to his house in Gibeah; the two destinations remain distinct.
No further seeing until the day of his death, Samuel's mourning and the Lord's regret at making Saul king remain.
column3: The death pronoun's antecedent and relation to later encounters need review; regretted represents metemelethē and is not automatically equated with parakeklemai at verse 11.

column2: The Lord challenges continued mourning, states rejection of Saul's reign, commands a filled oil horn and sends Samuel to Jesse at Bethlehem because He has seen a son to reign for Him.
Samuel's fear of being heard and killed by Saul receives the command to take a heifer in his hand and announce sacrifice; no invented account of concealment is added.
Jesse's invitation precedes God's promised instructions and anointing of the indicated person; the identity remains withheld until later speech.
Samuel obeys everything, arrives in Bethlehem and meets terrified elders who ask whether his arrival is peaceful; seer remains their form of address.
Peace, sacrificial purpose, consecration and rejoicing today precede consecrating and inviting Jesse and his sons; rejoicing is retained as an explicit command.
The arrival and sight of Eliab prompt the inference that His anointed is before the Lord; the line remains Samuel's judgment before correction.
column3: Surely interprets alla kai as emphatic assertion here; the particle combination and unnamed seeing/speaking subject remain questions, not proof of divine endorsement.

column2: Propose For before the explanation that God's seeing differs from human looking. Appearance, bearing of height, rejection, face and heart remain in their explicit contrast.
column3: Generic English presents render the Greek future forms in the maxim; no psychological definition of heart is inserted.

column2: Jesse calls Aminadab, who passes before Samuel; the response rejects this one too. The implicit speaker is contextually Samuel, without claiming his name is repeated in Greek.
Shammah is made to pass and also rejected; this second refusal remains separately worded rather than summarized with the others.
Seven sons pass before Samuel, who rejects selection among these; the count remains seven without reconciling later genealogical totals.
Propose behold before the youngest son's tending the flock. Are these all the boys? expresses whether the boys have run out; fetching him precedes the strong refusal to recline until arrival.
The youngest is brought, described as ruddy, beautiful-eyed and good to look upon before the Lord; the command explicitly names David and calls him good.
column3: The relationship of the dative Lord to the visual description is retained provisionally; good is not replaced by this is the one from another form.

column2: Samuel anoints among the brothers; the Lord's Spirit leaps on David from that day onward, and Samuel departs to Armathaim. The temporal continuity is explicit.
The Lord's Spirit leaves Saul and an evil spirit from the Lord chokes him. The source's agency and bodily verb remain without clinical diagnosis or theological paraphrase.
Propose Behold for the servants' presentative diagnosis of an evil spirit of the Lord choking Saul. The attribution is retained as their speech.
The servants seek their lord a skilled kinyra player, whose playing during the spirit's presence will bring wellbeing and rest; the instrument and both promised effects remain.
column3: No modern instrument identification or medical mechanism is asserted; the spirit is called evil here without adding an absent of the Lord phrase.

column2: Saul asks for a properly playing man to be found and brought; please expresses the request particle without changing his human authority.
Propose Behold before the servant's eyewitness report. Jesse's Bethlehemite son is skilled, discerning, warlike, wise in speech, good in appearance and accompanied by the Lord; the full list remains.
Saul sends to Jesse for David specifically, identified as with his flock; the selected your flock is not omitted as redundant identification.
A gomor of loaves, wine skin and one young goat are sent by David's hand. Gomor is retained instead of introducing a donkey-load from another source.
Propose naming Saul as the inferred loving subject and David as the inferred equipment bearer so the English pronoun switches are clear. David's arrival and standing before Saul remain.
column3: These are contextual agency clarifications supported by Saul's request to retain David in verse 22; neither name is claimed as repeated at those two points in the Greek.

column2: Saul asks Jesse to let David stand before him because he found favor in Saul's eyes; the bodily favor image and request remain.
Repeated spirit episodes prompt David's hand-playing of the kinyra, Saul's refreshment and wellbeing, and the evil spirit's departure. The habitual sequence remains without a permanent-cure claim.
